entries.title: Minimal, Local, Causal Explanations for Jailbreak Success in Large Language Models
entries.summary: COLM 2026 paper introducing LOCA, a method that identifies a minimal set of interpretable, intermediate-representation changes that causally induce refusal on an otherwise-successful jailbreak. Evaluated on harmful original-jailbreak pairs across Gemma, Llama, and Qwen; LOCA achieves refusal with on average six changes where prior globally-oriented methods routinely fail after 20. Argues global explanations (e.g., 'jailbreaks all suppress a single harmfulness direction') are too coarse because different strategies and harm categories rely on different intermediate concepts.
entries.takeaway: Jailbreak success is not one global mechanism; per-attack, per-category local causal explanations require far fewer interpretable interventions to force refusal than global steering.

lessons.point: Global 'one direction encodes harmfulness' explanations of jailbreaks are incomplete: different strategies and harm categories exploit different intermediate concepts.
lessons.excerpt: different jailbreak strategies may succeed by strengthening or suppressing different intermediate concepts, and the same jailbreak strategy may not work for different harmful request categories (e.g., violence vs. cyberattack)

lessons.point: A local, per-instance causal explanation needs far fewer interpretable representation changes than global methods to induce refusal on a successful jailbreak.
lessons.excerpt: LOCA can successfully induce refusal by making, on average, six interpretable changes; prior work routinely fails to achieve refusal even after 20 changes.

lessons.point: Framed as a step toward mechanistic interpretability of jailbreaks in current chat models, with code released.
lessons.excerpt: LOCA is a step toward mechanistic, local explanations of jailbreak success in LLMs. Code publicly available at

actionable.title: Treat 'the model has one harmfulness direction' as an oversimplification when reasoning about jailbreak defenses
actionable.detail: When evaluating a refusal probe or steering-based defense, do not assume that suppressing a single harmfulness direction covers all attack families. LOCA-style local explanations suggest defenses should be tested per-attack-family and per-harm-category; single-direction interventions may work for one class of jailbreak and miss another. This does not license a stronger claim yet — the paper reports averages across a benchmark on 3 open chat models, not a general result about frontier models.

entries.prior_art: Extends the linear-representations / refusal-direction line (e.g., Arditi et al. on refusal directions, Zou et al. on RepE) by moving from global to local causal explanations of individual jailbreak successes.
entries.threat: Not a direct threat report; describes a diagnostic method. The implicit threat is that global 'refusal direction' defenses may leave whole strategy/category subspaces uncovered, so red teams can find jailbreaks that survive single-direction ablation-based refusal probes.
entries.conditions: Applies to open-weight chat models where intermediate representations are accessible (evaluated on Gemma, Llama, Qwen). Findings are on a benchmark of harmful original-jailbreak pairs; extrapolation to frontier hosted models is not established.
entries.mitigations: When claiming a jailbreak defense generalizes, evaluate it per strategy class and per harm category rather than only on aggregate refusal rate. Include mechanistic red-team probes that verify the defense actually blocks the specific concept the attack strengthens/suppresses, not just the global harmfulness axis.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts copied verbatim from data/_raw/mrscan-b011-0.txt. Related claims (jailbreak-transfers-across-models, prompt-injection-is-a-permanent-attack-surface) exist in the ledger. Novelty is moderate — local causal explanations extend an active research line rather than opening a new axis. Relevance kept moderate because this is a mechanistic-interpretability paper on open chat models, not a production defense recipe.

entries.title: Self-state attacks: corrupting an agent's own memory and config uses legitimate syscalls
entries.author: Yimeng Chen et al.
entries.summary: Self-hosted agents read and write their own memory and configuration files, so once an attacker can write to that state the corruption itself is performed with legitimate OS system calls - the malicious step does not look anomalous at the OS layer. The authors formalize a four-axis attack space, realize 43 operations on real self-state files injected into traces from a representative self-hosted agent, and find a layered defense covers most cells with a small residual that stays structurally indistinguishable. Note the precondition: this assumes the attacker already has local write access; the paper does not address how that access is obtained.

lessons.point: Given an attacker who can already write to an agent's state files, the corruption step is performed with legitimate system calls - so the malicious action itself carries no distinguishing OS-level signal. This is a post-compromise finding, not a new access path.
lessons.excerpt: An agent may get compromised via corruption of its own state -- a compromise realized via legitimate OS system call invocation.

lessons.point: Layer the defense by state type: access-control prevention on instruction and configuration layers, workload-conditioned detection on the memory layer, periodic backup for recovery.
lessons.excerpt: a layered defense stack (access-control prevention on the instruction and configuration layers, workload-conditioned detection on the memory layer, and periodic backup for recovery) is effective on most attack cells

lessons.point: For a small residual subset of attack cells, OS-level signals alone are structurally insufficient to separate malicious from legitimate state changes - even though the layered stack handles most cells. Plan for recovery, not prevention alone.
lessons.excerpt: a small residual attack surface remains structurally indistinguishable at the OS level

entries.threat: An attacker with write access to an agent's instruction, configuration, or memory files redirects its behavior persistently, without exploiting the agent or the OS.
entries.conditions: Self-hosted agents persisting memory and configuration to the local filesystem, AND an attacker who has already obtained local write access to those files (e.g. via prior code execution).
entries.mitigations: Apply mandatory access control to instruction/config files, use workload-conditioned detection on memory files, and take periodic backups so recovery is possible for the undetectable residual.
entries.takeaway: Treat an agent's memory and config files as protected assets with their own access-control and backup policy - once an attacker can write them, the corruption step itself looks legitimate.
entries.prior_art: Agent memory poisoning and config tampering have been discussed piecemeal. The contribution is systematizing the space (four-axis, 23-cell matrix) and measuring which cells OS defenses cover - not a new attack capability, since it presumes existing local write access. 'Self-state attacks' is the authors' own coinage in this paper. Preprint, not peer-reviewed.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: surfaced the unstated precondition - the attacker must already hold local write access, making this post-compromise systematization rather than a new access path; 'representative' agent not 'real'; novelty 73->45.

editorial.reason: Part of the live agent-security cluster with a directly actionable hardening step: apply access-control and backup to an agent's own memory/config files.

entries.title: ASTELD: A Six-Axis Classification Framework for Autonomous AI Agents
entries.summary: Proposes ASTELD, a six-axis classification framework for autonomous AI agent platforms (Architecture, Security, Tool integration, Execution, Level of autonomy, Deployment), evaluates it on eight platforms with OpenClaw as case study, classifies 50+ OpenClaw derivatives, and derives a six-category vulnerability taxonomy plus a claimed empty region: local-first deployment combined with enterprise-grade security.
entries.takeaway: If you are picking an agent framework, force yourself to place it on the six ASTELD axes and check whether the security axis matches your deployment topology; the paper claims the local-first-plus-enterprise-security quadrant is empty in current systems.

lessons.point: There is no shared classification for comparing agent platforms across architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, which makes framework choice ad hoc.
lessons.excerpt: Autonomous AI agent platforms differ substantially in architecture, security, tool integration, execution, autonomy, and deployment, yet the field lacks a common classification scheme for comparing these design choices.

lessons.point: Cross-platform patterns include a security-accessibility diagonal and strong execution-architecture coupling, so security posture correlates with other design axes rather than being an independent knob.
lessons.excerpt: The resulting profiles separate all eight platforms under their dominant configurations and reveal three cross-platform patterns: a security-accessibility diagonal, strong execution-architecture coupling, and capability convergence with persistent architectural differentiation.

lessons.point: None of the surveyed autonomous-agent platforms combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security, which the authors flag as an under-served design region.
lessons.excerpt: The analysis also exposes a consequential empty region: none of the evaluated systems combines local-first deployment with enterprise-grade security.

actionable.title: Use ASTELD's six axes as an agent-platform intake checklist
actionable.detail: When admitting a new autonomous-agent platform, record its ASTELD coordinates (Architecture, Security, Tool integration, Execution, Autonomy/human-control, Deployment) plus the six-category vulnerability taxonomy from the OpenClaw case study; treat mismatches between the security axis and your deployment topology as a blocking finding.

entries.prior_art: Synthesizes prior agent taxonomies with observable platform properties; complements Invariant Labs tool-poisoning framework and NIST-style STRIDE-adjacent AI threat models.
entries.threat: Agent platform choice is made without a systematic security-axis comparison, so security assumptions from one deployment topology are silently carried over to another (e.g. cloud-managed to local-first) where they do not hold.
entries.conditions: Organization is selecting or extending an autonomous-agent platform; multiple platforms considered without a shared axis vocabulary; security posture treated as independent of architecture and deployment.
entries.mitigations: Score candidate platforms on all six ASTELD axes; use the six-category vulnerability taxonomy from the OpenClaw case study as an intake checklist; flag any framework whose Security axis is inconsistent with its Deployment axis for further review.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim from arXiv abstract; related_claims cross-checked.

entries.title: AegisShield: Democratizing Cyber Threat Modeling with Generative AI
entries.summary: AegisShield is a GenAI-assisted threat modeling tool that combines STRIDE, MITRE ATT&CK, NVD, and AlienVault OTX to auto-generate threats for small organizations. Evaluated on 243 expert-graded threats and 8000+ AI-generated ones, it reduced complexity, produced output semantically aligned with expert threats, and mapped 85.4% of threats to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.
entries.takeaway: GenAI-assisted STRIDE plus a live NVD/OTX feed can plausibly reach an 85% MITRE ATT&CK mapping rate on generated threats; this is a viable base pattern for lightweight threat-modeling assistants, but the human-vs-AI validation is against a modest 243-threat expert set.

lessons.point: GenAI-assisted STRIDE + MITRE ATT&CK can achieve ~85% technique-mapping rate on auto-generated threats.
lessons.excerpt: achieves an 85.4 percent success rate in mapping threats to MITRE ATT&CK techniques

lessons.point: Feeding live threat intelligence (NVD, AlienVault OTX) into the LLM tightens the generated threat descriptions.
lessons.excerpt: By integrating real time threat intelligence from the National Vulnerability Database and AlienVault Open Threat Exchange, AegisShield produces streamlined and accessible threat descriptions.

lessons.point: GenAI outputs were semantically aligned with expert-developed threats on a 243-threat expert benchmark.
lessons.excerpt: yields outputs semantically aligned with expert developed threats (p less than 0.05)

actionable.title: Prototype: STRIDE + MITRE mapping assistant hydrated by NVD/OTX
actionable.detail: For internal threat-modeling assistants, feed live NVD and OTX advisories into the LLM system prompt and require STRIDE category + ATT&CK technique ID per generated threat, then measure technique-mapping accuracy against a small expert-labeled set.

entries.prior_art: Applies STRIDE + MITRE ATT&CK with LLM assistance; similar to prior LLM-assisted threat modeling but adds live threat feeds and evaluates against expert-labeled threats.
entries.threat: Small organizations skip formal threat modeling; auto-generated threat models risk over-trust in LLM output, missed threats, or hallucinated MITRE technique IDs that look authoritative.
entries.conditions: Use of an LLM to generate STRIDE threats; mapping produced by an LLM without independent verification; consumer organization lacks security staff to sanity-check output.
entries.mitigations: Require LLM-generated threats to cite a specific NVD CVE or OTX pulse; check MITRE technique IDs against the ATT&CK JSON as a post-step; keep a human-in-the-loop review before adopting the generated model as a control baseline.

entries.title: Scientific computing in the age of agentic AI
entries.summary: OpenAI's field report on eight agent-assisted scientific-computing projects (five using Codex only, three combining Codex and Claude Code, primarily in life sciences) reports a consistent pattern: agents shift the human's job from implementation to verification and orchestration — defining what to build, specifying how to measure correctness, and deciding when a project ships. The security-relevant lessons are (a) agents express confidence even on clearly wrong output, so groundedness has to come from an external reference (parity with an existing tool, simulated data with known answers, statistical checks), (b) initial implementations are fast but resolving edge cases and numerical differences dominates elapsed time, and (c) lower implementation cost fragments maintainership — today's rewrite is tomorrow's abandoned code without an explicit steward. The transferable claim for agent harness design is that verification-side infra (acceptance tests, reference outputs, iterative benchmarks) is the actual bottleneck once agents are cheap.
entries.takeaway: Once agents are cheap, verification is the bottleneck: acceptance tests, parity references, and named maintainers are the new critical infrastructure — not more agent capability.

lessons.point: Agents produce confident-sounding output that contains clear errors; the strongest defense is an external reference with a measurable acceptance target — parity with an existing tool, simulated data with pre-computed answers, or bounded statistical behavior.
lessons.excerpt: agents handled specific, well-scoped requests effectively but could not reliably judge whether their work was scientifically valid or met expectations. Indeed, agents often expressed confidence even when their work contained clear errors. Human reviewers therefore needed to find reliable ways to validate the results. The strongest approaches used an external reference or measurable acceptance target such as exact output agreement, parity with an existing tool, appropriate statistical behavior, or answers established in advance using simulated data.

lessons.point: The role shift is verification/orchestration, not authoring: humans set the goal, define correctness metrics, and gate ship — a re-partitioning that dictates where evaluation infra has to live in an agent-assisted org.
lessons.excerpt: Contributors consistently describe a shift in the researchers’ role from implementation to verification and orchestration: specifying what to build, defining how to measure correctness, and deciding when a project is ready to ship.

lessons.point: The last-mile is where the elapsed time actually sits: fast first implementations, slow edge-case and numerical-diff resolution — an argument against benchmarking agents on first-pass throughput and for benchmarking on time-to-ship-quality.
lessons.excerpt: Agents often produced initial implementations quickly, but resolving edge cases and subtle numerical differences took much longer. Completing the “last mile” of an implementation often took the most work.

lessons.point: Cheap agents create a maintainership fragmentation problem: rewrites split communities and expert attention, so a rewrite without a named owner and credible maintenance plan is a future abandonment liability.
lessons.excerpt: But lower implementation costs also make it easier to produce many similar rewrites, fragmenting users and spreading the expert attention required to keep any one tool reliable. That makes long-term stewardship and attribution essential.

actionable.title: Verification-first harness pattern for agent-assisted engineering work
actionable.detail: Codify the OpenAI field-report pattern for any team standing up an agent-assisted engineering loop: (1) before any agent runs, define an external reference — parity target, simulated dataset with known answers, or bounded statistical property — that will actually decide 'ship or not', (2) break the goal into small feedback-driven iterations with intermediate benchmarks so the agent's confident-but-wrong pattern gets caught early, (3) explicitly assign a human owner for last-mile edge cases (numerical diffs, format oddities) because the field-report data says this dominates elapsed time, and (4) attach a maintenance/stewardship plan at the same moment you commit the rewrite — no rewrite without a named owner and a credible support line, or it becomes future abandoned code.

entries.prior_art: First-party OpenAI messaging on agentic coding productivity has been ongoing across 2026. The delta of this specific report is the eight-project retrospective corpus (five Codex-only, three Codex+Claude Code), the explicit naming of verification acceptance patterns (parity, simulated-answer, statistical), and the stewardship / abandonment framing. The verification-bottleneck claim overlaps with the pool's 'human review catches agent PR risk' claim and PortSwigger's HTTP Terminator human-in-cascade pattern.

entries.title: TOFD: Target-Oriented Feature Decoupling against Poisoning Attacks in Split Federated Learning
entries.summary: Proposes TOFD, a three-stage defense against poisoning attacks in Split Federated Learning: Target Inference via class-specific Margin Perturbation, Sample Purification of poisoned smashed data, and Decoupling Optimization using an adversarial guidance model. Reports SOTA robustness across five datasets with low compute overhead.
entries.takeaway: Split Federated Learning has attack surfaces (the split boundary and smashed activations) that generic FL defenses miss; TOFD exploits the split paradigm itself for detection.

lessons.point: Split Federated Learning's split architecture creates attack surfaces distinct from vanilla FL, and most existing defenses fail to exploit the split paradigm.
lessons.excerpt: its split architecture introduces unique attack surfaces, rendering it vulnerable to diverse poisoning attacks. Most existing defenses fail to exploit the split paradigm, limiting their ability to detect and contain malicious behaviors at an early stage.

lessons.point: TOFD's Sample Purification stage filters poisoned smashed data using thresholds calibrated from class-specific Margin Perturbation.
lessons.excerpt: Sample Purification, which adaptively filters poisoned smashed data using thresholds calibrated through cross-class min-max normalization of MP

lessons.point: Reported to outperform SOTA defenses across five datasets with low overhead — an empirical, not just theoretical, claim.
lessons.excerpt: Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that TOFD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art defenses under diverse attack scenarios, achieving superior robustness with low computational overhead suitable for practical deployment.

actionable.title: If deploying Split Federated Learning, generic FL poisoning defenses may under-protect
actionable.detail: Teams shipping Split Federated Learning should not assume vanilla FL defenses (Krum, trimmed mean, coordinate-wise median) transfer — the SFL split creates novel attack surfaces at the smashed-data boundary. Review split-aware defenses like TOFD before production.

entries.threat: Poisoning attacks against Split Federated Learning that manipulate smashed activations at the split boundary, evading generic FL defenses which do not model the split.
entries.conditions: Applies specifically to Split Federated Learning deployments (server-side model split, client-side feature extraction, smashed data transferred across the split). Empirical claims are based on five academic datasets; production generalization is unverified.
entries.mitigations: Three-stage TOFD pipeline: (1) Target Inference to identify likely attack targets via class-specific Margin Perturbation; (2) Sample Purification that adaptively filters poisoned smashed data; (3) Decoupling Optimization using an adversarial guidance model to suppress residual adversarial effects.
entries.prior_art: Extends the FL-poisoning-defense literature (Krum, Trimmed Mean, FLAME, SparseFed) into the Split FL setting, which has attracted growing attention as SplitNN deployments emerge.

entries.title: Corrupting Attention: Evasion-Based Adversarial Attacks on Encoder Attention in Detection Transformers
entries.summary: Introduces the first attack that directly optimizes an encoder-attention objective on detection transformers under a bounded L-infinity perturbation, driving the model's own attention toward a corrupted target rather than injecting an attacker-owned sink token. Reduces DETR-R50 mAP on COCO from 42.1 to 0.97 (roughly 4x stronger than the strongest prior attack under identical budget) and generalizes across four qualitatively distinct attention-corruption objectives and to DINO-Swin-L.
entries.takeaway: Attacking the encoder-attention structure itself in detection transformers is a stronger evasion strategy than perturbing outputs, and the weakness generalizes across corruption objectives and both dense and deformable attention formulations, suggesting the attention structure is the root vulnerability.

lessons.point: The attack directly optimizes an encoder-attention objective under an imperceptible bounded perturbation, rather than targeting detection outputs.
lessons.excerpt: we introduce the first attack that directly optimizes an encoder-attention objective under an imperceptible, bounded ℓ∞perturbation.

lessons.point: It reduces DETR-R50 mAP on COCO from 42.1 to 0.97, roughly a 4x reduction over the strongest prior attack at identical budget.
lessons.excerpt: Our attack reduces DETR-R50 mAP on COCO from 42.1 to 0.97, a ∼4×reduction in resulting mAP over the strongest existing attack under an identical perturbation budget and iteration count.

lessons.point: The vulnerability generalizes across four distinct corruption objectives and both dense and deformable attention, implicating the attention structure itself.
lessons.excerpt: across four qualitatively distinct targets, dispersion, re-ranking, permutation, and peak-suppression, detection consistently drops below 3 mAP, suggesting that the weakness arises from disrupting the attention structure itself rather than from any single target.

actionable.title: Note attention-structure attacks against DETR-class detectors
actionable.detail: For safety-critical CV systems using DETR-family detectors, treat encoder attention as an exposed attack surface: adversarial patches that target attention (not detection outputs) generalize across corruption objectives and across dense/deformable attention. Defenses evaluated only against output-space attacks under-estimate risk.

entries.prior_art: Prior adversarial-detection attacks that target the detection output rather than attention; patch-based attacks that introduce a visible attacker-owned sink token are the explicit comparison.
entries.threat: Imperceptible L-infinity-bounded adversarial perturbations at inference time against DETR-family object detectors deployed in safety-critical systems (e.g., autonomous driving, surveillance).
entries.conditions: White-box or transfer access to a detection-transformer model where the attacker can produce bounded input perturbations; deployment context relies on detection mAP for downstream decisions.
entries.mitigations: Evaluate detector robustness with attention-targeted attacks, not just output-space attacks; consider certified-robust or attention-regularized training; treat detection outputs as attacker-influenceable when input pixels are untrusted.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim; unicode chars for L-infinity and approximation are preserved as-fetched. This is classical CV adversarial ML, not LLM prompt injection, so cluster E (prompt injection and adversarial) is not the right fit; no cluster covers CV adversarial evasion. cluster=null.

entries.title: Online Security Learning in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems under Hidden Byzantine Attacks
entries.summary: Theoretical/algorithmic paper on cooperative multi-agent control where a hidden fixed subset of agents are Byzantine and can stealthily overwrite their own coordinates of the team's planned joint action after seeing the plan. Shows attacker information determines geometry (observing attacker => (s,a)-rectangular robust MDP; blind attacker => s-rectangular). Proves an information-theoretic lower bound (indistinguishable horizon-one instances force Omega(K) security regret while return regret is zero) and gives a stage-tied robust estimator with regret bound O~(H^2 sqrt(SAK)) + E[D_K].
entries.takeaway: Security regret in Byzantine cooperative MAS cannot be reduced below a cumulative response-gap term; the achievable bound depends on what the attacker can observe about the planned action.

lessons.point: The attacker's observational power sets the robust MDP structure, changing what defenders can achieve.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker that observes the planned action induces an exact (s,a)-rectangular robust Markov decision process (MDP) whose rows are convex hulls of overwrite-induced public-outcome laws, whereas a blind attacker induces an s-rectangular model.

lessons.point: There is an unavoidable dependence on a cumulative response-gap term in security regret.
lessons.excerpt: Two indistinguishable horizon-one instances force Ω(K)expected security regret while return regret is zero, showing that dependence on D Kis unavoidable.

actionable.title: Model attacker observability before choosing robustness bounds in MAS
actionable.detail: When designing multi-agent robustness guarantees, calibrate the robust-MDP model to what a compromised agent can observe about the joint plan; assuming a blind attacker yields weaker (s-rectangular) guarantees than the true (s,a)-rectangular geometry when plans are visible.

entries.prior_art: Robust MDPs (Nilim & El Ghaoui; Iyengar); Byzantine multi-agent RL; s- vs (s,a)-rectangularity.
entries.threat: A hidden fixed subset of cooperative agents observes the team's planned joint action and stealthily overwrites its own action coordinates before execution; the learner never sees the overwrite or the executed action, only planned actions plus public rewards and states.
entries.conditions: Cooperative online multi-agent control with public planned actions, public rewards, and public states; unknown subset of Byzantine agents with plan-observation capability; no direct observability of executed joint action.
entries.mitigations: Model the attack as an (s,a)-rectangular robust MDP when plans are observable to the attacker; use a stage-tied robust estimation-to-decisions learner with regret O~(H^2 sqrt(SAK)) + E[D_K]; accept an unavoidable cumulative response-gap term in security regret.
entries.verify_note: Excerpts verified verbatim (including the paper's own inline unicode/formatting artifacts) against data/_raw/mrscan-b020-4.txt.

entries.title: Algebraic Cryptanalytic Extraction on Hard-Label Neural Networks
entries.summary: The paper reformulates Carlini et al.'s (EUROCRYPT 2025) hard-label neural network extraction attack into an algebraic framework and introduces an Approximate Signature Vector (ASV) method that replaces expensive SVD-based rank checking with inner-product operations, reducing clustering complexity from O(n^2 (d^k)^3) to O(n (d^k)^3) on average. It also presents the first hard-label extraction attack against max-pooling CNNs using a kernel-centric clustering scheme, demonstrated on a 64-64x4-10 FCNN and LeNet-5.
entries.takeaway: Hard-label neural network extraction is getting materially cheaper: an inner-product-based Approximate Signature Vector replaces SVD in dual-point clustering, and max-pooling CNNs are no longer out of reach for hard-label cryptanalytic attacks.

lessons.point: The 2025 SOTA hard-label extraction attack was polynomial in theory but bottlenecked in practice by O(n^2 (d^k)^3) SVD-based clustering; replacing SVD with inner products drops the average cost to O(n (d^k)^3).
lessons.excerpt: its dual-point clustering relies on singular value decomposition (SVD) with a time complexity of O(n 2⋅(d(k))3), resulting in huge runtime in practice

lessons.point: The ASV method exploits two structural properties of trained networks: near-orthogonality of high-dimensional random vectors and disentangled feature learning in practical DNNs.
lessons.excerpt: high-dimensional random vectors are nearly orthogonal, and neurons in practical DNNs tend to learn disentangled features

lessons.point: The paper claims the first hard-label model extraction attack against max-pooling CNNs, achieved by switching from neuron-centric to kernel-centric clustering that leverages convolutional weight sharing.
lessons.excerpt: this paper presents the first model extraction attack against hard-label max-pooling Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) by proposing an advanced ASV method with a kernel-centric clustering scheme instead of the neuron-centric clustering

actionable.title: Model extraction on hard-label APIs is getting cheaper; treat top-1 label endpoints as leaky
actionable.detail: Assume that black-box endpoints exposing only the top-1 label of small-to-medium FCNNs and now max-pooling CNNs are extraction-vulnerable at feasible cost. Rate limit, add query-pattern anomaly detection, and prefer prediction-confusing outputs (top-k with noise) if secrecy of weights matters.

entries.prior_art: Carlini et al., Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Network Models, EUROCRYPT 2020 and follow-ups through EUROCRYPT 2025.
entries.threat: An adversary with hard-label black-box access to a deployed neural network can extract functionally equivalent parameters at materially reduced runtime, previously infeasible in practice due to SVD cost.
entries.conditions: Target must be an FCNN or a max-pooling CNN accessible via a hard-label prediction API; adversary can issue enough queries to run dual-point clustering.
entries.mitigations: Query rate limiting, per-user query budgets, adding output noise, moving from hard-label to top-k probability outputs only where product allows, monitoring for boundary-probing query patterns.

entries.title: Quantigence: A Multi-Agent Framework for Post-Quantum Security Analysis on Commodity Hardware
entries.summary: Quantigence is a supervisor/worker multi-agent framework built on a 4-bit-quantized 9B model that runs on a single commodity GPU (8 GB budget) for post-quantum crypto (PQC) security analysis, grounded in arXiv, NVD, and a local NIST-PQC index. On atomic single-fact benchmarks a single tool-using agent already reaches 98% accuracy vs 57% zero-shot, and multi-agent decomposition does not improve over that; on complex multi-faceted queries, the supervisor/worker split raises rubric coverage from 78% to 89%. The paper also measures retrieval-corpus poisoning robustness.
entries.takeaway: Tool access dominates the accuracy jump on single-fact queries; multi-agent decomposition only pays off on multi-faceted questions where rubric coverage matters, not on lookups.

lessons.point: Tool access, not multi-agent structure, drives accuracy on atomic single-fact queries.
lessons.excerpt: tool access is what raises accuracy, from 57% (zero-shot) to 98% (single agent), and a single tool-using agent is, as expected, a strong baseline that multi-agent decomposition does not beat on single-fact lookups.

lessons.point: Supervisor/worker decomposition helps on complex multi-faceted queries via rubric coverage, not on simple lookups.
lessons.excerpt: the supervisor/worker decomposition instead improves rubric coverage from 78% to 89% and judged answer quality.

lessons.point: The framework is explicitly evaluated for robustness to retrieval-corpus poisoning, not just accuracy.
lessons.excerpt: we report both, and further measure robustness to retrieval-corpus poisoning and behavior across model scales.

actionable.title: Don't add agent layers where a single tool-using agent already saturates the task
actionable.detail: Benchmark a single tool-using agent before spinning up planner/worker decomposition. Reserve multi-agent orchestration for tasks whose evaluation criterion is rubric coverage on multi-faceted queries, not atomic-fact accuracy.

entries.title: Trustworthy Agent Network: Trust in Agent Networks Must Be Baked In, Not Bolted On
entries.summary: SIGKDD 2026 Blue Sky Ideas position paper arguing that Agent-to-Agent (A2A) networks introduce systemic vulnerabilities (adversarial composition, semantic misalignment, cascading operational failures) that per-agent alignment techniques cannot cover, and that trust must be designed into the coordination framework from the start rather than retrofitted. Proposes a four-pillar conceptual framework but is a vision paper without a concrete protocol or evaluation.
entries.takeaway: A2A network trust is a coordination-layer problem: individual-agent alignment does not compose, so agent-network protocols need trust primitives designed in from the beginning.

lessons.point: Multi-agent A2A networks introduce classes of vulnerabilities that single-agent alignment cannot address.
lessons.excerpt: they introduce systemic vulnerabilities, such as adversarial composition, semantic misalignment, and cascading operational failures, that existing agent alignment techniques cannot address

lessons.point: Retrofitting trust onto protocols designed for individual agents is insufficient; trust needs to be a first-class property of the coordination framework.
lessons.excerpt: the trustworthiness of A2A networks cannot be fully guaranteed via retrofitting on existing protocols that are largely designed for individual agents. Rather, it must be architected from the very beginning of the A2A coordination framework.

lessons.point: The paper proposes a four-pillar conceptual framework as a design vision, not a concrete protocol or empirical evaluation.
lessons.excerpt: We present a comprehensive conceptual framework that situates trust in A2A systems through four design pillars.

actionable.title: When adopting an A2A protocol, ask what trust primitives are in the protocol vs. bolted on later
actionable.detail: For teams evaluating an A2A or agent-mesh protocol (Google A2A, Anthropic MCP-of-agents patterns, custom orchestrations), treat trust primitives — identity, capability scoping, semantic-mismatch handling, failure containment — as protocol-level acceptance criteria rather than application-level responsibilities. The paper does not prescribe a specific mechanism, so this is a review posture, not a checklist.

entries.prior_art: Overlaps with earlier A2A security taxonomies and the general 'security must be designed in, not bolted on' thesis applied to distributed systems for decades. Similar to Google's A2A protocol design goals and multi-agent alignment literature.
entries.threat: Agent-network compositions can be attacked in ways single-agent defenses do not cover: an adversarial agent joining a network, semantic drift across agent hand-offs, or a fault in one agent cascading through downstream tool calls.
entries.conditions: Applies to production systems that connect multiple heterogeneous LLM agents (potentially across organizational trust boundaries) into coordinated workflows using shared protocols.
entries.mitigations: The paper proposes trust be architected via four design pillars in the coordination framework rather than added later, but does not commit to a specific mechanism. Practical takeaway: require identity, capability scoping, and failure-containment at the protocol level before opening an agent network across trust boundaries.

entries.title: PolicyGuard: Prompt-Configurable Semantic DLP for LLM Coding Agents
entries.summary: PolicyGuard is a pre-model interception framework that classifies user prompts against a plaintext natural-language policy file, positioned as an alternative to regex/model-fine-tune/vendor-classifier DLP. Reports 96.5% effective block rate at 3.0% false-positive rate on 927-prompt frozen test, 100% accuracy on 217-prompt hidden holdout, and 86.4-96.5% EBR across four LLMs without policy changes. Paper has been withdrawn by the author pending institutional review.
entries.takeaway: The policy-as-prompt pattern (DLP rules as an editable natural-language file, evaluated by an LLM) is worth prototyping for coding-agent input filtering, and the reported numbers cross-model without policy edits are strong. But the paper is withdrawn pending institutional review, so treat the specific numbers as unverified until it reappears; use the pattern, not the benchmark.

lessons.point: Rule-configurable natural-language DLP policies outperform equivalent content expressed in JSON, and dramatically outperform zero-shot classification.
lessons.excerpt: PolicyGuard's natural language format significantly outperforms equivalent content in JSON format (McNemar chi-squared = 31.58, p <0.001) and dramatically outperforms zero-shot classification (Cohen's h = 0.915)

lessons.point: A single natural-language policy can port across four different LLMs at 86.4-96.5% effective block rate without modification.
lessons.excerpt: the same policy achieves 86.4-96.5% EBR across four different LLMs without modification

lessons.point: The paper is currently withdrawn pending an institutional review process, so headline numbers should not be cited as settled.
lessons.excerpt: This paper is being withdrawn because it was submitted prior to completion of a required institutional review process. The authors intend to resubmit after the review is complete

actionable.title: Track PolicyGuard resubmission before adopting its numbers; the pattern is still useful
actionable.detail: Prototype the policy-as-prompt pattern (plaintext policy file consumed as an LLM classification prompt) for coding-agent input DLP where regex is too rigid. Do not cite the 96.5% EBR / 100% holdout numbers in decisions until the paper is un-withdrawn after institutional review.

entries.prior_art: Contrasts with regex-based DLP, fine-tuned classifiers, and vendor-managed DLP; sits alongside NeMo Guardrails, LlamaGuard, and similar LLM-based content classifiers.

entries.conditions: Coding agent accepts free-form NL prompts; DLP is expected to enforce customer-specific policy without model retraining.
entries.mitigations: Deploy a pre-model LLM classifier reading a plaintext policy file; A/B test against regex DLP on your own prompt distribution; do not rely on the reported cross-model portability numbers until the paper is republished.

entries.title: TensorZero Gateway: a request parameter that overrides the server's object-storage config gives arbitrary file read and SSRF
entries.summary: TensorZero's /internal/object_storage endpoint accepted a caller-supplied storage_path that dynamically overrode the gateway's configured object-storage backend. Selecting the filesystem backend turns it into arbitrary file read; selecting s3_compatible turns it into SSRF toward internal and cloud-metadata endpoints. Textbook bug class, worth logging only because LLM gateways keep shipping optional auth alongside endpoints whose /internal prefix is doing the authorization.

lessons.point: The bug class is 'the caller picks the backend': whenever a request field selects a storage driver or endpoint, the caller has inherited a server-side trust decision, and the two sinks are always the same - local file read and outbound SSRF.
lessons.excerpt: The `/internal/object_storage` endpoint accepts a caller-supplied JSON `storage_path` parameter that dynamically overrides the TensorZero `[object_storage]` configuration.

lessons.point: A path prefix is not an authorization boundary. `/internal` only means internal if something enforces it; here exposure hinges entirely on whether the operator turned authentication on.
lessons.excerpt: If a developer's TensorZero deployment has authentication enabled, only authenticated callers can exploit this vulnerability.

lessons.point: Durable control for anyone running an LLM gateway: default-deny egress from the gateway to link-local and RFC1918 ranges, so a storage-backend confusion bug cannot reach cloud metadata even when it exists.
lessons.excerpt: the caller can coerce the gateway into making outbound object storage requests to attacker-chosen internal/cloud-metadata endpoints

entries.takeaway: LLM gateways are ordinary web services with an unusual amount of credentials on disk - audit them for caller-selectable backends before anything AI-specific.
entries.threat: An untrusted caller reads gateway-local credential files or pivots to internal/cloud-metadata services through the gateway.
entries.conditions: Gateway reachable by untrusted callers; the advisory states exploitation is limited to authenticated callers where authentication is enabled.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 2026.6.0; block external access to /internal/object_storage; enable gateway authentication; restrict egress.
entries.prior_art: Caller-controlled S3-compatible endpoint override -> SSRF (repeatedly patched in MinIO-integrating and self-hosted file services); CWE-73 external control of file path via selectable storage driver; Capital One-era cloud-metadata SSRF; Spring Boot Actuator /env config-override exposure. The only new facts are the product, endpoint and version.
entries.verify_note: Verifier scored novelty 12/100 - 'the conceptual delta over prior art is approximately zero', same primitive, sinks, fix and workaround as a decade of prior bugs, and it does not even carry the LLM-specific wrinkle (no prompt-injection-reachable path). Also corrected: the advisory says files that MAY contain credentials, does not demonstrate metadata retrieval, states exposure as a precondition rather than an observed fact, and gives no CVE/CVSS/affected range. Held for review as derivative.
